- L6.1: Characterization: x appears in the sequence iff gcd(x, a_i) > 1 for every i (equivalently for every earlier term, or every minimal term).
- L6.2: Large-prime erasure, for all terms: membership depends only on the small primes (at most a_1^2). Includes the warning that pairwise intersection alone doesn't imply this (family F_k counterexample).
- L6.3: Periodicity from n = 1: membership depends only on a mod L with L the product of the small primes; T is the number of residues that appear; a_{n+T} = a_n + L for every n >= 1.

Field mapping:

- "reduction" = (C) characterization. The write-up proves that acceptance depends only on support, and the self-duality: m >= a_1 is accepted iff gcd(m, every earlier accepted term) > 1. Actually the write-up establishes: "an integer m ≥ a_1 is accepted exactly when supp(m) contains at least one member of C" — which is the characterization. Also "acceptance depends only on the support" claim. Let me check whether that claim is correctly proven.

The claim: Suppose a_1 ≤ x < y and supp(x) = supp(y). If x is rejected, it has a smaller accepted coprime witness, which is then also coprime to y; hence y is rejected. If x is accepted, every accepted integer smaller than y is noncoprime to x, because accepted integers are pairwise noncoprime. Having same support as x, y is noncoprime to every earlier accepted integer, so y is accepted.

Hmm, wait: accepted integers pairwise noncoprime: gcd(x, z) > 1 for accepted z, means supp(x) ∩ supp(z) ≠ ∅, so supp(y) ∩ supp(z) ≠ ∅, so gcd(y, z) > 1. Yes correct. Accepted integers are those accepted by the greedy scan, each accepted integer is noncoprime to every earlier accepted integer. Hence any two accepted integers are noncoprime (the later one is noncoprime to the earlier one). Yes.

Actually wait, a_1 itself is accepted trivially. Every subsequent one is noncoprime to a_1 at least.

So the reduction (C) is established: acceptance depends only on the support, and acceptance criterion is gcd with every earlier accepted integer. That's L6.1 essentially. Yes, this equivalence is standard and correct. The write-up asserts "Indeed, this is precisely the minimality condition in the definition of a_{n+1}." That's a brief justification but it's essentially fine. It's a correct argument (though terse). I'd count it as established.

- "lower_bound" = (F) finiteness / large-prime erasure. The write-up proves finiteness of C via sunflower lemma and weight descent (Lemma 1 and Lemma 2). Setup: F = family of supports of accepted integers (among integers ≥ a_1; acceptance depends only on support). Self-duality (1): S ∈ F iff S meets every member of F. The proof of (1):

Lemma 1: For every K, only finitely many C ∈ C with |C| ≤ K. Proof via infinite sunflower lemma: infinite family of distinct sets of size ≤ K has infinite subfamily with pairwise intersection a fixed set R (a Δ-system/sunflower with core R). OK.

H ∩ S = ∅: since y coprime to w(S) which has support S. Yes.

w(H) ≤ ∏_{q | y} q ≤ y < w(S) = w(E \ {p}).

Given support-dependence, for a nonempty finite prime set S, either all integers ≥ a_1 with support S are accepted or all rejected. So F = {S : all m ≥ a_1 with supp(m) = S are accepted}. Fine.
